6.1.m: — Having bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, / and to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then proclaim the "Jaya."
To him by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance / was opened with the stick of knowledge-collyrium, salutation to that glorious guru.
The sages said: / The Pātālakhaṇḍa has been heard, as narrated by you, O best among the knowers, / endowed with various stories and bestowing supreme bliss.
Now we wish to hear what increases devotion to the Blessed Lord. / Whatever remains here in the Padma [Purāṇa], tell that out of grace, O guru.
Sūta said: / Listen, all you sages, to what was indeed spoken by Śaṅkara / to Nārada when he questioned him—wisdom that destroys sins.
Once Nārada, beloved of the Blessed Lord, wandering through the worlds, / went to Mount Mandara to ask Śambhu about something in his mind.
Bowing to the lord of Umā seated there, by Śiva's command / he was seated upon a designated seat facing the almighty Lord.
Nārada said: / He asked the Lord this very thing that you ask of me, O best of men: / "O Blessed Lord, lord of the gods of gods, lord of Pārvatī, teacher of the world!
Instruct me on that by which knowledge of the truth of the Blessed Lord may arise." / Śiva said: / "Listen, Nārada, I will relate the Purāṇa equal to the Vedas,
hearing which one is freed from all sins, there is no doubt about this. / First there is the praise of the North, and the story of the mountains;
likewise the story of Jālandhara, and next the one named Śrīśaila; / the exposition of Haridvāra, and likewise that which sprang from the foot of Viṣṇu;
I will tell you of the sacred place Prayāga, and the Daśāśvamedhika; / and the greatness of Tulasī, and the conch, discus, mace, and others;
likewise the story of Dvārakā, then the rule for great festivals; / and the merit arising from tanks, step-wells, ordinary wells, water-kiosks, and so on;
then I will tell of the Gāṇapatya and the Vaiṣṇava scripture; / the glorification of temple-renovation, and the confluence with the Mandākinī;
the glorification of the Sābhramatī, and the glorification born of its bank; / the duty of women and śūdras, and what must be worn by those to be rejected;
the Thousand Names declared in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśa, / brought from Kailāsa by the first-born Nārada.
It should be recited with concentrated minds by people—by brāhmaṇas and especially by kṣatriyas, / and especially by women and śūdras.
This supreme, pure, meritorious [hymn] increases life; / it should be especially recited; one attains union with Viṣṇu.
That purifying Thousand Names of Viṣṇu is famous throughout the earth. / Here one should describe the abodes of the twenty-four forms;
and I shall tell their parents, and their intermediate forms, / and their lineage, Vedas, and their deeds here as well;
I will describe their women, according to the vision of wisdom; / the efficacy of the twenty-four Ekādaśīs and Dvādaśīs;
and the glorification of the Godāvarī, and the wearing of the conch, discus, and other marks— / especially their formal wearing by brāhmaṇas;
and the glorification of the Yamunā, and of the Gaṇḍikā, O sage; / and I will certainly tell the glorification of the Vetravatī;
the merit arising from the Gillitīrtha, and the great Śilākṣetra— / I will declare all that in the section named Uttara;
the glorification of Arbudeśvara, and the sacred places there; / and the glorification of the Sarasvatī, and the Siddhakṣetra and other sites;
the origin of Padmanābha, and the wearing of tulasī; / the glorification of gopīcandana, and the worship of the silk cloth;
the glorification of the Stainless One, and the vision of wisdom; / the offering of lamps there, and especially the offering of incense;
then the glorification of Kārttika, and the glorification born of Māgha; / and the glorification of all vows, according to the rules.
Listen, Nārada, I will tell of the excellent one named Jagannātha, / seeing whom a person is freed from sins such as slaying a brāhmaṇa;
where the food cooked and consumed bestows [benefits in] the next world, / where brāhmaṇas skilled in the Vedas and Śāstras eat—
what to speak of other people, O you of good vows! / There are twenty-five serpent[-like] female dancers of various kinds;
the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, the slaying of a child, and likewise the slaughter of cows— / all those go to destruction upon the sight of Jagannātha.
A creature uttering 'Jagannātha' is freed from great sins; / I will also speak of the worship of Viṣṇu with flowers and its glorification;
the description of mountains, and the description of countries; / the glorification of cow-worship, and the worship of the perfected beings;
whatever merit lies in giving boiled rice, I will declare all that; / the gift of the plantain heart, and thereafter the gift of trees;
the gift of horses, the gift of elephants, and the supreme glorification of chanting; / the tradition of mantra-initiation, and the characteristics of the guru;
the characteristics of a disciple are declared as the reciters of the Purāṇas know; / the glorification of water washed from the feet, and the śrāddha to the ancestors;
the gift on the death anniversary of ancestors, and the rule for releasing a blue bull; / the eclipse of the moon and sun, and whatever gift may be made then;
the glorification of giving a śālagrāma stone, and of garlands and scents; / the overlapping of the tenth day with the eleventh, and the twelfth day, the day of Hari;
and the glorification of these, and the names of Rudra; / the glorification of Mathurā, and likewise Kurukṣetra;
the story of the Setubandha, and that born of Śrī Rāmeśvara; / the glorification of Tryambaka, and the fruit of Pañcavaṭī;
the glorification of the Daṇḍaka forest—listen, O best of brāhmaṇas; / the glorification of the Daṇḍaka forest and the cause of Nṛsiṃha's appearance;
the glorification of the Gītā, and likewise of the Bhāgavata; / the glorification of the Kālindī, and the description of Indraprastha;
the deeds of Rukmāṅgada, and the greatness of the Vaiṣṇava, / and when a single meal is eaten by a Vaiṣṇava—listen, O best of brāhmaṇas.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving away the earth with its oceans, / that very fruit one completely obtains when even a single Vaiṣṇava is fed.
The sattvic are endowed with sattva; the rajasic are held to be lustful; / the tamasic are declared to be base: such is the classification of Vaiṣṇavas.
Those who are brāhmaṇas, Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to the duties of the Vedas, / their glorification I will explain as it was told, O Nārada.
Those who take pleasure in reviling Viṣṇu out of greed for wealth, O best of men, / their sin I will declare right now, O best of sages.
And the narrative of Jvālāmukhī, and the viewing of the snow-mountain, / and that place where the origin of Brahmā occurred, I declare.
The origin of the Kāyasthas, the explanation of Gayā, / the nature of Gadādhara, and the description of the Phalgu [river],
and the glorification of these, as seen and heard in the Padma [Purāṇa], / the nature of Mahābodha, and the renown of Kalki,
the glorification of Rāmagayā, and what arose at Pretaśilā, / and the narrative of Brahmā and the narrative of the stone, I shall tell;
and the story of Brahmayoni, and of the fig tree named Akṣaya, / whatever great merit there is in performing a funeral oblation there—all that I shall relate;
and the devotion shown to Maheśvara by high-souled Viṣṇu, / on account of which Mahārudra, even today in Kāśī, chants the praise of the Faultless One.
Then I shall speak of the glorification of the ocean, O Nārada, / the merit arising from libations of sesame, and the merit arising from barley,
and the libation offered to the gods along with basil leaves— / that glorification I shall fully tell as it was spoken to me by Brahmā;
the glorification of the sound of the conch, and the countless merit [thereof];
the glorification of Sunday, and of the conjunction named Viṣṇu, / the glorification of Vaidhṛti, and likewise of Vyatīpāta;
all this I shall declare as it was told, O Nārada: / the gift of food, the gift of clothes, and likewise the gift of land,
the gift of a bed, the gift of a cow, and likewise of a bull, / the glorification of Janmāṣṭamī, and the glorification of the Fish [avatar],
the glorification of the Tortoise that was told, and likewise of the Boar, / and the glorification of gifts such as cows, I declare.
Those devotees led by Prahlāda who are renowned on earth, / their greatness I shall declare from then on; listen, O best of divine sages!"
the greatness of the night-vigil, and that of offering a lamp, / the distinct fruit of worship during the watches of the night, O best of divine sages;
and the narrative of Paraśurāma, and the killing of Reṇukā, / and the gift of land made to brāhmaṇas by Rāma;
the merit born of Rāma's hermitage I declare without remainder, / likewise the account of the Narmadā, and of the meritorious rites of worship;
the gift of the Vedas and the Purāṇas, the definition of the stages of life, / the merit of gifting gold, and the gift of the cosmic egg;
the gift of the Padma Purāṇa, and the manifestation of its sections: / the first is the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, and the second is the Bhūmikhaṇḍa;
the third is the Svargakhaṇḍa, and the fourth is named the Pātāla; / the fifth is declared as the Uttara—these are the sections in succession.
This Padma Purāṇa was composed by high-souled Vyāsa / for the welfare of the world and for the good of brāhmaṇas.

It generates merit for śūdras, destroys dire poverty, / bestows liberation and happiness swiftly, grants prosperity, and is imperishable; / having heard it, one should make a gift according to the prescribed rule, O Nārada.

6.2.m: Maheśa said: / There are one hundred and twenty-five thousand mountains; / among them, the supreme Badrikāśrama possesses great merit,
where the god Nara-Nārāyaṇa dwells, O Nārada. / His true form and splendor I shall explain here and now.
On the peak of the snow-mountain, in dark form, O twice-born, / both persons, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, abide there;
one person is white, while the other is dark. / Those who make an effort toward the Himālayas go along that path.
The great lord is reddish-white in color and wears matted locks; / and this dark Nārāyaṇa is the source of the universe, the supreme lord,
four-armed, exalted, splendid, manifest, unmanifest, eternal. / At the northern course of the sun, great worship takes place there, O virtuous one.
For a period of six months or so, worship does not take place at all; / it is then covered in snow as long as the southern course lasts.
Therefore, such a deity has not existed nor will ever exist. / There the gods dwell, as well as the hermitages of the sages;
sacred fires and the Vedas—their sound is constantly heard there. / Sight of him should indeed be obtained; it destroys millions of murders.
Where the Gaṅgā is [known as] the Alakanandā, there one should perform ablutions. / Having bathed there, one is indeed released from great sins,
where the divine Viśveśvara dwells beyond any doubt. / On one occasion, O brāhmaṇa, I performed severe austerities.
Then the divine Nārāyaṇa, compassionate to his devotees, / the imperishable Supreme Person, the Lord incarnate, whose banner is Garuḍa, / well-pleased, said to me: 'Choose a boon, O virtuous one!'
The venerable Nārāyaṇa said: / 'Whatever you desire, O god, that very wish I grant. / You are the lord of Kailāsa in bodily form, Rudra, the protector of the universe.'
Rudra said: / 'O god Janārdana, since you are well-pleased, I accept with contentment. / If you wish to grant, let two boons be given to me:
may I always have devotion to you, and may I become a king among devotees; / and may all the worlds say, "This one is ever his devotee."
By your grace, O Lord of gods, may I become a bestower of liberation; / of those people who worship me, I shall be the bestower [of liberation], no doubt.
May I be renowned in the world as a devotee of Viṣṇu; / to whomever I become a boon-giver, may liberation be his, O Lord.
Wearing matted hair and with limbs smeared with ashes, in your presence / may I become renowned in the world by the grace of your feet.'

6.3.m: Sūta said: / Once the brāhmaṇa Nārada went to the Kāmyaka forest / to see the Pāṇḍavas emaciated by sorrow, and was honored by them in accordance with rule.
Then, having bowed to the best of sages, Yudhiṣṭhira said: / 'O lord, by what action have we fallen into this ocean of sorrow?'
The sage said to him: 'Abandon your sorrow, O son of Pāṇḍu! / In worldly existence, an aggregate of joy and sorrow, what mortal is happy?
Even the Lord is not permanently stationary; he is afflicted by bodily aggregates. / No embodied being is free from grief, because an embodied being endures grief.
Because the sun has a body, mighty Rāhu swallows it; / and Rāhu's head was severed by Śauri at the consuming of nectar.
Even that divine bearer of the Śārṅga bow was hurled into the ocean abyss / by the heroic Jālandhara, who was also slain by Śambhu.'
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / 'Who is that heroic Jālandhara? Whose son was he, and whence his power? / How did he whose banner is a bull slay Jālandhara in battle?'
Tell me all this in detail, O ascetic! / Being thus addressed by the king, Nārada related:
Nārada said: / Hear, O king, the divine tale that destroys the mass of all sins, / and the exceedingly wondrous battle between Īśāna and the son of the ocean.
Once, Indra, the chastiser of Pāka, went to praise Giriśa, / surrounded by a host of apsarases and encircled by many gods.
Surrounded was the god by gandharvas skilled in the technique of the lute. / Rambhā, Tilottamā, Rāmā, Karpūrā, and Kadalī,
Madanā, Bhāratī, and Kāmā, adorned with every ornament, / and other dancing women came near the gods.
The gandharvas, yakṣas, and siddhas, along with Nārada and Tumburu, / and the kinnaras constantly arrived, as did the kinnara women.
Vāyu and Varuṇa, Kubera the giver of wealth, / Yama, Agni, Nirṛti, and the other hosts of deities;
Maghavan mounted on a heavenly chariot, the celestial women seated in heavenly chariots, / and the gods riding their own mounts went swiftly to Kailāsa.
Then the gods beheld Kailāsa, the supreme mountain, / an ornament, as it were, of all the mountains and of the earth;
bestowing joy on every side, pure, standing like a mass of perfections, / where the trees are wish-granting trees and the stones grant desires;
the mountain adorned with punnāgas, nāgacampakas, / tilakas, devadārus, aśokas, pāṭalas, mangos, and mandāras,
where the winds carry the fragrance of the surrounding forests, / and those Malaya breezes become sluggish from their extensive wandering;
ponds with steps of crystal, containing deep, pure waters, / with lotuses resembling gold attached to stems of lapis lazuli,
Where the radiance of white water-lilies shines in every direction; / ponds adorned with kahlāra lilies, surrounded like rubies.
set with emeralds, surrounded everywhere with topazes, / paved with ruby stones, and variegated with various minerals.
They saw that most beautiful mountain, fashioned to surpass heaven; / having seen Kailāsa, the foremost mountain, they were filled with wonder.
Alighting from their heavenly chariots, Maghavan and those deities / then approached Nandin the gatekeeper and spoke these words:
“O best among the foremost of the gaṇas, listen to my supreme word! / Announce quickly [to the Lord] that I have come here for dancing,
to Īśvara, the lord of gods, surrounded by all the deities.” / Hearing Indra’s words, Nandin spoke to Giriśa:
“O Lord, this Devarāja, Puraṃdara, has arrived with all [the gods] / for the purpose of dancing.” Then he said to him: “Bring quickly the husband of Śacī.”
Then Nandin ushered in Vāsava along with the gods. / Seeing Giriśa, the god whose banner bears a bull, he praised him.
Then all those dancing women, headed by Rambhā, in the presence of Hara, / joyfully performed dances with drums, lutes, and musical instruments.
Taking brass cymbals, flutes, keeping time, and trumpets, / they engaged in the enthusiasm of dance, and the god Puraṃdara himself
performed an exquisite dance, hard even for gods to attain. / Īśvara, attaining satisfaction, spoke these words to Vāsava:
“I am pleased, O best of gods; choose a boon of your choice!” / When the lord of gods had spoken thus, [Indra,] proud of the strength of his own arms,
spoke in reply to Hara: “I choose a battle / where there is a warrior equal to you; grant me such a fight, O Lord!”
Having spoken thus, the victorious [Indra] departed, having obtained a boon from lord Śambhu. / When Śakra had gone, Giriśa then spoke these words:
“O my gaṇas, listen to my words: the king of gods has become exceedingly proud!” / Having spoken thus, Hara became filled with anger.
Then anger became manifest, standing embodied before him, / resembling dense darkness; then the anger spoke to Mṛḍa:
“Give me your instruction: what may I do for you, O Lord?” / The lord of Umā then said: “Go and conquer Vāsava,
having reached the celestial river and being full of the ocean’s potency.” / Being thus addressed, the anger vanished; those gaṇas were filled with wonder.
When the union of the ocean took place with desire in the cosmic age of Īśāna, / the river of heaven was then intoxicated with the heat of the fullness of her own youth.
Seeing her, the king of the ocean became filled with surging waves; / then, O best of kings, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean took place.
Reaching that great river, he took delight with his own strength. / Thereupon, in the meantime, a great warrior was born from the ocean.
A powerful son was born from the ocean in that great river. / As soon as he was born, O king, by that son of the great ocean
crying out, the earth was shaken and the three worlds resounded. / And the four-faced one abandoned the posture of deep meditation.
In the meantime, seeing those three worlds terrified, / Dhātṛ, at the words of the king of gods, went to the great ocean.
Thinking “This is a wonder,” mounted on a swan, he went with speed. / Seeing Brahmā arrived, the ocean offered worship. / Then Brahmā said to him: “Why are you roaring in vain, O ocean?”
The ocean said: / “I am not roaring, O lord of gods; my son is powerful, O Lord. / Protect the child, for the sight of you is difficult to attain.
Let the son be seen!” He said to his exceedingly beautiful wife, / and she, by her husband’s command, went with the son near Brahmā.
Placing the son on the lap of the four-faced one, she bowed down at his feet. / Then, seeing that wondrous son of the ocean, wonder indeed arose in the Creator.
When Viriñci could not release the hand of the child who had grasped his beard, / then the ocean, laughing, approached, holding the beard and releasing the child's hand.
Seeing such prowess of that child, the Self-born / affectionately said “Jālandhara!” By name he became Jālandhara.
Then Prajāpati affectionately gave him a boon: / “This Jālandhara shall become invincible to the gods;
by my grace, he shall enjoy heaven along with Pātāla.” / Having spoken thus, Brahmā swiftly mounted his swan and disappeared.

6.4.m: Nārada said: / That boy, gradually growing in childhood, / leaping into the lap of the wind, would run toward the ocean.
Devoted to sport, he captured the cubs of lions and placed them in cages; / thus his prowess was fit for war, fighting with lions and elephants.
Springing up from there into the sky, he would bring down birds to the earth; / with his roars, he terrified heaven along with the ocean.
All the hosts of living creatures within the ocean, O king, / were devoured by the son of the ocean, and out of fear of him they hid themselves.
Seeing the water bereft of living creatures, the submarine fire, out of fear of him, / abandoned its own place and entered the Himālaya.
Gradually casting off childhood, that son of the ocean, / having then attained early youth, assaulted heaven by his prowess.
Once the son of the Ocean said to his father, the sea: / 'Give me, father, a very spacious place suitable for my dwelling.'
Understanding his son's speech, the great ocean replied: / 'Son, I will give you a kingdom, or whatever is difficult to obtain on earth.'
Thereupon the guru of the Daityas, Bhārgava, went to the Ocean. / Seeing him arrive, the Ocean duly worshipped him.

Then, seated on that seat given by the lord of rivers, radiant with the splendor of gems possessing great beauty, / he somewhat surpassed the radiance of the lotus-born [Brahmā] on the lovely peak of Sumeru of brilliant luster.
Folding his hands in reverence, the Ocean said to the poet [Śukra]: / 'By good fortune is your arrival here; tell me, what may I do?'
Then the poet [Śukra], the teacher of the Daitya race, said to the Ocean: / 'What is the use of someone born at all, if he merely robs his mother of her youth,
and does not shoot up like a banner at the front of his own family? / Your son will surely enjoy the three worlds through his prowess.
In Jambūdvīpa there is a great seat served by hosts of yoginīs / that is now flooded by you; release the dwelling of Jālandhara.
Give that realm to this son, O great ocean; / residing there, he will be invincible and unslayable.'
Addressed thus with affection by Bhārgava, the Ocean then effortlessly / withdrew for the love of his son, and displayed dry land in the water.
A hundred yojanas wide and three hundred [yojanas] long was / that holy land Jālandhara, celebrated by his very name.
Summoning Maya, the foremost among Daityas, the Ocean said: / 'Build a city at the seat of Jālandhara for Jālandhara.'
Spoken to thus by the Ocean, he indeed built a city made of jewels, / with ramparts, city-gates, doors, stairways, houses, and terraces,
where peacocks dancing on the palace roofs inlaid with sapphires / mistook them for a gathering of rain-clouds.
Where the rays rising from mansions of coral and ruby / were sought by birds, mistaking them for lovely mango shoots.
Where, seeing the fires of the golden palaces, / frightened peacocks fled, suspecting forest fires.
Where the directions, mingled with the radiance rising from crystal mansions, / shone like the ocean with foam churned by Mount Mandara.
Where women, their faces resembling the full moon at dusk, / standing in the bright light on their mansions, caused bewilderment.
Where breezes delighted by gardens of Indranīpa and Kādamba trees, / entering the minds of women, produced a fever of passion.
Where people, seeing the sexual union of men depicted in paintings, / found their own eagerness for pleasure with their beloveds truly doubled.
Where, from the streaks of incense smoke billowing from windows, / the sky became like the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Kālindī.
Where, through the radiance arising from numerous houses, the entire sky / shone like a high autumn cloud filled with rainbows.
Where the horses of the sun, weary and agitated by perpetual movement, / found rest at midday standing atop the palaces.
Where on the mansions here and there, the noble women wearing garlands of jasmine / shone at night like constellations.
Where the sound produced by the friction of chains of golden swings / clearly made the beautiful earth appear like the land of Meru.

6.4.m:
Together with the rivers and with Uśanas [Śukra], the Ocean / performed the coronation of his son there, accompanied by musical instruments and his own roaring.

Which the self-born god [Brahmā] himself declared unto Skanda upon the conquest of Tāraka, / and which Vācaspati [spoke] to the beloved of Śacī [Indra] at the great festival of his imperial reign in heaven.

with those auspicious speeches, which are swans on the lake of the wonderful mouth of Viriñci [Brahmā], we pray for blessing at the time of the wedding of the earth with the festive recitations of mantras.
The great ocean gave to his son Jālandhara a formidable army / of a thousand mahāpadmas, born from his own belly.
Śukra too affectionately gave him his own lore, / called Mṛtasaṃjīvanī, the illusion that deludes Rudra,
and the other sciences of weapons and missiles, according to rule, to the ocean's son; / whatever else there was, the poet-sage then expounded to him.
Then the ocean, having consecrated his son Jālandhara, / departed to his own abode in a divine body, surrounded by rivers.
Jālandhara, seeing the divine city adorned with city-gates, / moved about with Śukra, well worshipped by hosts of twice-born.
In the meantime, the mighty daityas residing in Pātāla, / all headed by Kālanemi, came to Jālandhara.
Then the mighty warriors appointed the daitya Śumbhāsura / as the commander of his army, which was like the Milk Ocean.
Having brought the army under his control and made the waters firm on the earth, / Jālandhara then ruled the kingdom given by his father.
Meanwhile, there was formerly in heaven an apsaras named Svarṇā; / by the grace of Krauñca she had a daughter named Vṛndā.
The beauty that was created separately by the Creator, endowed with splendour, / was formed into the body of Vṛndā in order to see it brought together in one place.
That Vṛndā, exquisitely fair-limbed, an enchanting woman who deluded people, / Svarṇā gave for Jālandhara to Śukra who asked for her.

6.4.m:
Śukra said: / With this beauty, a wondrous weapon to the eyes of the world belonging to the god of love, / O woman of thighs like plantain stems, live long and be happy!

Having fashioned her himself, astonished in his mind, the Creator set the pinnacle / of the labor of his work upon one who was the essence of beauty.
When he is not seen, women make the god of love their husband; / obtain that warrior with long eyes, the limit of what is to be seen, as your husband!
The ocean's son married Vṛndā / by the gāndharva marriage; they became husband and wife, delighting the people, O king.
Fickleness was abandoned by her, and Jālandhara too, / by conduct suited to mature action, did not desire another's wife.
Once, seated in the assembly, seeing Rāhu whose head was cut off, / he asked the Bhārgava: 'Why does this one have only half a body remaining?'
He recounted to him the former event from the beginning: / how the Milk Ocean was churned by the gods for the sake of nectar.
Hearing that, the asura Jālandhara was amazed and spoke, / his face gracious: 'Rāhu, become capable of taking any form at will now!'

Thus, by the counsel of Śukra, the mighty son of the ocean, / remembering his paternal uncle, waged war against the gods, like a hero.

Thus [ends the chapter] named 'The Marriage of Vṛndā and the Consecration of Jālandhara' in the story of Jālandhara, in the dialogue between Nārada and Yudhiṣṭhira, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.5.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Who was the uncle of the ocean's son? What happened in his war? / How did that daitya fight? Tell me that, Nārada.
Nārada said: / Listen, O tiger among kings! The uncle of Jālandhara / was the Milk Ocean; by churning it, wealth was taken away by the gods.
Formerly, Lakṣmī, the moon, nectar, the serpent, and the horse were taken by the gods and asuras; / hearing that, the asura Jālandhara waged war against the gods.
Once the mighty one sent a messenger named Durvāraṇa / to the palace of the king of the gods, having instructed him what to say.
Then Durvāraṇa, mounting a chariot, went to heaven; / wishing to enter the palace, he was stopped at the door by the gatekeepers.
The messenger said: / 'I have come as the messenger of Jālandhara into the presence of Śakra; / you should go there and announce me.'
Hearing his words, the messenger went at that very moment to the lord of Śacī, / prostrated himself, and said: 'O god, I have returned from the earth.'
The gatekeeper, replied to by the great Indra with 'Bring the messenger', / took that messenger by the hand and brought him near Vāsava.
Durvāraṇa, having entered the assembly of the gods, beheld / Hari surrounded by thirty-three crores of gods,
on a divine golden throne, served by the breeze of chowries, / with a thousand lotus-eyes blossoming from the nectar-sentiment of Śacī's love.
Then Durvāraṇa, seeing the lord of the gods together with his guru, / bowed out of his own pride, smiling at the splendour of his eyes.
He took the seat assigned to him, that messenger of Jālandhara. / 'Whose [messenger] are you? For what purpose have you come?' Hari said to him.
The messenger said to Puraṃdara: 'I am the messenger of Jālandhara; / he is the king of all the worlds; hear his command from my mouth:
"Why was my uncle, the Milk Ocean, churned by you / using Mount Mandara, and his treasury of immense wealth plundered?
Lakṣmī, the moon, nectar, the serpent, the horse, that jewel, the coral and the rest— / surrender everything, and quickly abandon heaven, O Puraṃdara!
So, at my word, quickly do everything as is proper; / beg pardon of that king, if you wish to live!"'
Then laughing, Maghavan said to Durvāraṇa: / 'Listen, messenger, in brief to the reason for the churning of the ocean.
Formerly, the son of the Himālaya named Maināka was my enemy; / he was held in his belly by that stupid ocean.
And the fire in the form of a horse, by which moving and unmoving beings were burned, / that too was harboured by that wicked-souled ocean.
He is indeed the refuge and lord of the dānavas, enemies of dharma; / he constantly gives curds, ghee, and milk to the dānavas.
For this very reason he was churned by us, O Durvāraṇa, / and punished, and his fortune was taken away by the ancient gods.
Listen, messenger: he was dried up with his relatives by my brāhmaṇa, / the pot-born [Agastya]; what is more, this one is afflicted by bad company alone.
Even if he comes with his whole army to fight us, / he will indeed meet with destruction at that very time.'

Having spoken thus, the slayer of Vṛtra ceased; the messenger of the river-lord's son / went and reported aloud to the son of the ocean all that had been said by the lord of the gods, from the beginning.
Nārada said: / Hearing the words of the great Indra through the mouth of his own messenger, / the son of the ocean, enraged, summoned his entire army.
The daityas residing in Rasātala and those living on the surface of the earth / came there with their forces at Jālandhara's command.
At the outset of the march of the ocean's son's army, with their roars, / the sky, Pātāla, and all the quarters cracked, O king.
Having faces of horses, elephants, and camels; fearsome with cat-faces; / with faces of tigers, lions, and rats; with eyes like lightning;
with serpents for hair, huge-bodied, some having swords as body-hair, / and others running around, roaring with the sounds of clouds.
Crowded with chariots, elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers, radiant with multitudes enjoying battle, / led by hundreds of millions of commanders, that entire army then shone forth, O king.
There was an aerial chariot extending a hundred yojanas, yoked with ten million swans, / filled with a multitude of thousands of splendours, stocked with every kind of object.
Mounting that aerial chariot, Jālandhara set out at once; / at midday on the first day, he reached Mandara along with his forces.
Cut up by the carriers of palanquins and crushed by many elephants, / he reached Meru on the second day together with his army.
That great army encamped on the peak in Ilāvṛta; / then the chiefs of the Daityas broke the Khāṇḍava and Nandana groves.
The peaks of Meru were shattered by the foremost of Dānavas; / having fastened swing-platforms onto Santānaka trees,
the foremost Daityas disported themselves along with the wives of the Siddhas. / With the saffron of breasts, betel, sandalwood, aloe ornaments,
and flowers fallen from braids of hair, the river of Meru was filled. / The eastern region of Sumeru was crushed by his elephants,
and they traversed the southern [region] with chariots, and the northern and western with soldiers. / Then the Asura Jālandhara dispatched the Daityas.
Others went to the peak of Mahendra with sounds of kettle-drums; / having shattered the city of the king of kings [Kubera], and of Yama and Varuṇa,
and of the other world-protectors, they arrived at Amarāvatī. / Then portents occurred in heaven—celestial, terrestrial, and atmospheric.
Abundant dust fell, a mass of darkness expanded, / and then the thunderbolt fell lusterless from the hand of Indra.
Seeing the frightening omens in heaven, Mahendra spoke thus to his guru: / 'What shall we do, and to whom shall we go for refuge? Look, that battle is upon us.'
Then Vācaspati spoke words to the lord of the thirty [gods]: / 'Seek refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu, who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha.'
Thus addressed by the preceptor, Ākhaṇḍala [Indra] went swiftly with the gods to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha, / seeking refuge with the enemy of Kaiṭabha.
Vijaya, the doorkeeper, reported to Vāsudeva: / 'All the gods, terrified by fear of Jālandhara, have arrived.'
Śrī said: 'He is my brother and must not be killed by you when you fight for the sake of the gods; / bound by an oath out of love for me, O Lord, he must not be fit for slaying.'
Hearing the glorious words, Viṣṇu, the protector of the three worlds, / then mounted Garuḍa, whose flapping wings covered the sky.
Quickly departing from the dwelling of Vaikuṇṭha, Hari then saw the gods / terrified by fear of Jālandhara and devoid of luster.
All those gods saw Hari resembling a dense cloud, / having four arms adorned with the Śārṅga bow, the conch, the mace, and the lotus.
Reciting a hymn of praise before him, Indra said: 'By the son of the lord of rivers, / by Jālandhara, heaven has been shattered, O God.'
Hearing that speech of Indra and granting freedom from fear to the dwellers of heaven, / Hari, the destroyer of Asuras, shone forth together with the gods to conquer the Asura.
Then Vāsava [Indra], mounting the chariot brought by Mātali, / advanced ahead of Vāsudeva, holding the thunderbolt.
On the left were all the gods, and on the right came / the beloved of Svāhā [Agni] on the right side, seated on a ram.
Jayanta, the son of Śakra [Indra], having mounted the elephant Airāvata, / and Indra [mounted on] Uccaiḥśravas, both went before the Lord.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga, / Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is considered the tenth,
then Tvaṣṭṛ, then the blessed Viṣṇu, the youngest-born, shone forth; / thus these twelve Ādityas stood before Indra.
Vīrabhadra, Śambhu, Giriśa of great renown, / Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, Aparājita,
Bhuvanādhīśvara, Kapālin, O ruler of men, / Sthāṇu, and the blessed Bhaga—these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.
Śvasana, Sparśana, Vāyu, Anila, and Māruta, / Prāṇa, Apāna, and Sajīva: these eight Maruts stood before him.
Vivasvat too marched in their midst in twelve forms; / then the lord of the Kiṃnaras, Dhanada, advanced, mounted on a palanquin.
The Rudras, mounted on bulls, and Māruta, riding a deer, / went before the army, armed with tridents and iron clubs.
The Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Guhyakas, / bearing every kind of weapon, marched in the vanguard of the entire army.
The eastern and western oceans were overrun by the troops; / on that [field] Hari, the king of the earth, moved about in the form of the Boar.
Having arrived with speed from heaven desiring to slay the Daitya army, / the northern flank of Sumeru was surrounded by the army of the gods.
And the wondrously heavy host of Jālandhara / swiftly took up position, occupying the southern flank from the golden peak.
Prepared in a day and a night in that realm of Ilāvṛta, / the battlefield was established between Meru and Mandara.
There, filled with joy, the Dānavas swiftly went to the ground / that promised victory to them as told by the sage [Śukra], and the gods went to that declared by their Guru [Bṛhaspati].

With chariot champions, and surrounded by surging elephants pouring streams of rut like clouds, / with boundless horses running ahead like Garuḍa, and with foot soldiers, the battlefield shone crowded.
Then arose the roar of musical instruments from both armies, / and the clamour of heroes roaring at one another.
Then a frightful battle took place between the Dānavas and the gods, / a crushing clash of the entire army, like the destruction of the three worlds.
Overcome by fear and utterly exhausted, Śruti lamented repeatedly, / [the field] then deprived of chariot shapes and completely filled with arrows.
The sky shone, its hairs bristling, shaking its garment of dust, / crying aloud in fear, as it were, with the terrible shrieks of birds.
Then, ordered by the lord of the gods, the clouds headed by Saṃvartaka, / mounting high upon elephants, fought the Asuras in the battle.
The Gandharvas and Kinnaras became horse-riders of the gods; / the Sādhyas and Siddhas were charioteers, and the Yakṣas and Cāraṇas rode elephants.
The Kiṃpuruṣas and wind-eating serpents were foot soldiers; / and the lord of diseases, King Consumption (Yakṣman), was the general of Yama.
There a very fierce battle took place between the Dānavas and the diseases; / the Daityas, fallen to the ground, writhed in agony from colics, fevers, and sicknesses.
Struck down by the Dānavas, diseases fell on the forefront of the battle, / while some maladies fled toward the mountains.
There were natural medicinal herbs, foremost among them the arrow-extracting herb (Viśalyakaraṇī); / cured of their wounds by these, Yama's servants fought on among the troops.
Struck down by the Dānavas with arrows, mallets, and double-edged axes, / the foot soldiers [fell] before infantry hosts with sharp swords and battle-axes.
Their bodies red with blood, they struck down one another by the millions; / then the horsemen on swift steeds hurled [their foes] into the sky.
Locking together, their bodies red with blood, they struck down one another; / a terrible throng of charioteers, covering the earth with hosts of chariots,
pierced great car-warriors with sharp arrows shot from bows; / with body and cheeks emaciated by rut, holding trunks tightly with trunks,
infuriated elephants hurled counter-elephants down to the earth's surface. / A certain Daitya, lifting a chariot with his two arms and leaping up, took to the sky;
he threw horsemen, horses, and elephants down to the earth's surface; / taking [a car-warrior] upon his shoulder, he went with speed towards Jālandhara.
Seizing two elephants in his armpits, a third upon his belly, / and holding a fourth upon his head, someone ran about in the battle.
Drawing his sword from the sheath and shaking the spotless sky, / an Asura advanced, striking down gods by the thousands in the fight.
A certain slender, full-breasted sky-roaming woman, eager for pleasure, / quickly descended from the sky and carried away a Daitya from the battleground.
She kissed his face, which was pierced by sharp iron arrows. / Then, binding the army of the gods, Kālanemi danced.
Then Janārdana, enraged, set forth against Kālanemi; / Yama against the hero Durvāraṇa, and Svarbhānu against the moon and sun;
the god Vaiśvānara went against Ketu; Bṛhaspati against Śukra; / the two Aśvins engaged there against the Daitya Aṅgāraparṇaka;
the son of Śakra went against Saṃhrāda; Dhanada against Nirhrāda; / Niśumbha was surrounded by the Rudras, and Śumbha by the Vasus in the combat;
the Viśvedevas came against Jambha, who stood like a cloud; / the Vāyus went against Vajraroman, and then Mṛtyu against Maya;
Vāsava, spear in hand, rushed eagerly against Namuci; / and the other Daityas too were surrounded by the gods who matched their respective valour.

6.6.m: Nārada said: / When duel combats had thus begun in many ways, / Hari, enraged, struck down Kālanemi with his mace.
Overcoming his swoon and composing himself, he struck Viṣṇu with arrows; / then, by the enraged Hari, he was hurled to the ground, lifeless.
O King, the Moon, collecting his wits, struck Rāhu with a sword; / but Rāhu, leaving him, then ran against the Sun.
Having vanquished the Thousand-Rayed One in battle, Rāhu ran towards the Moon; / and the Lord of the Night struck him with a sword in the battle.
Due to the hardness of the son of Siṃhikā's body, the sword was shattered to pieces; / then the Moon-Tormentor [Rāhu] struck him hard with a solid fist.
Lifting up the Moon and seizing him by the throat with speed in that great battle, / the Moon was swallowed by Rāhu, and then vomited out again.
Placing the deer, his own mark, upon his breast, he released him. / Seizing Uccaiḥśravas, the jewel among horses, the Moon-Tormentor
brought it near Jālandhara and offered it to him with devotion. / Durvāraṇa, enraged in the fight, struck Yama with a mace.
Pierced by sharp arrows by Śakra's son in the fight, / Saṃhrāda seized Jayanta, who was fainting from the blow of an iron club,
mounted Airāvata, and went towards Jālandhara. / Dhanada too killed Nihrāda with his mace in the battle.
With the impacts of their tridents, the Rudras forcefully struck Niśumbha; / and Niśumbha severely tormented them with a multitude of arrows.
The Asura Śumbha filled the hosts of gods with arrows; / Maya, full of magical power, bound Mṛtyu with nooses and led him away.
He gave him to Jālandhara, the son of Paulomī, and he in turn to the ocean; / and he was cast into the mouth of the ocean: may the world live fearless!
Having bound Namuci with nooses, Vāsava too led that slayer of the universe / down to the netherworld; then Jālandhara advanced.
Then, O King, a very fierce battle took place between Indra and Bala; / the radiances of Bala's body shone in the ten directions like ten suns.
All the weapons of Śakra shattered against Bala's body, / and Indra was struck in the chest by Bala, the stronger, with a club.
Then Indra let out a terrible roar; hearing that, Bala laughed. / And as he laughed, pearls dropped from his mouth.
Out of desire for that body, Vāsava did not fight then; / he excessively praised Bala, an ocean of strength.
[Bala] said to the foremost of gods, "Choose a boon!" Addressed thus, he said to Bala: / "If you are pleased, O lord of Daityas, you should give me your own body."

6.6.m:
Hearing Indra's words, he said to Bala: "Cut through [me] with weapons and take me. / What is not to be given by great-souled ones?

Like speech to one deaf, like a woman with rolling eyes to a blind man, / like a garland of flowers on others, wealth is useless to a miser.

Great-souled ones do not seize even enemies who harm them; / the rivers take their rival streams to the ocean, not to the mountain.

A virtuous person, intent upon the welfare of others, suffers no change even at the time of destruction; / a sandalwood tree, even when cut down, makes fragrant the edge of the axe.

Destiny is supreme; the body perishes, but wealth offered to the good does not perish; / of the cool-rayed moon, that very digit alone remains which is on the head of Śambhu.

They are the truly virtuous, the crest-jewels of the cosmic sphere, who show goodness toward those who do no favors. / When their purpose is served, people break off relations; even a wicked man devotes himself to those who previously injured him [only when it serves him].

Saying, "So be it," the thousand-eyed [Indra] struck Bala with a club. / Then his body did not break; Śakra was overcome with worry.
Reminded by Mātali, he struck that body with his thunderbolt. / By that blow of the thunderbolt, Bala's body shattered.
One part of Bala's body fell upon the golden mountain [Meru], / a second on the snowy mountain [Himavat], and a third fell upon Mount Go;
a fourth fell into the river of the gods [Gaṅgā], and likewise a fifth upon Mandara; / a sixth part, born of the limbs of Vijaya, fell into the diamond mine.
Of him whose birth was pure, by his thoroughly purified deed, / all the members of his body attained the state of seeds of gems.
From the thunderbolt, the scattered bone-fragments became six-cornered diamonds; / from both eyes came sapphires, and rubies were born from his ears;
from his blood came rubies, and from his fat came emeralds; / corals came from his tongue, and likewise his teeth became pearls;
the emerald born from his marrow became topaz, bronze from his nose, / silver from his feces, copper from his semen, and from his urine;
from the rubbing of his limbs arose brass and sacred gems; / from his sound arose cat's-eye gem, and very beautiful jewels likewise;
from his nails came the origin of gold, and from his blood the origin of mercury; / from his fat arose quartz crystal, and coral arose from his flesh.
The gems born from Bala's body that were on the surface of the earth / will be enjoyed by pure people through an abundance of accumulated merit.
Meanwhile, hearing that Bala had been killed in battle by Maghavan, / the queen named Prabhāvatī went to the vicinity of his feet.
Seeing her husband whose limbs were scattered on the battlefield, / Prabhāvatī lamented, her eyes filled with tears, her hair disheveled, her breasts firm:
"Alas, my lord, powerful and valiant, beloved in body, beloved of the world! / Why have you abandoned me and attained absolute liberation here?
Other embodied beings, knowing the body to be filled with old age, leprosy, and the like, do not abandon it; / but you, my beloved, have cast aside your body in vain!
O beloved, by your divine body a necklace is adorned; / by you, eager for battle, my braid was bound—

untie it yourself, O beloved, for me afflicted with the sorrow of widowhood!" / Seeing Bala's queen lamenting thus, the ocean-born one [Jālandhara], / filled with sorrow, said to Śukra: "O Bhārgava, bring Bala back to life!"
Śukra said: "He has met death by his own will; how am I to bring him back to life? / Even so, by the power of mantra he will utter speech."
Jālandhara said: "I wish to hear Bala's voice in person, O Bhārgava." / Addressed thus by Jālandhara, he became engrossed in meditation for a moment.
Then from his mouth arose a sound delightful to the ear, / distinctly directed toward Prabhāvatī, as if risen from a musical instrument:
"O Prabhāvatī, merge your body into my limbs!" / Hearing his words, Prabhāvatī became a river;

flowing eastward from Sumeru, she merged directly into Bala's limbs; / by her water, the supreme luster of the gems was produced.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, named 'The Ascent to Heaven by the Demon Bala,' in the story of Jālandhara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].

6.7.m: Nārada said: / Then the enraged Jālandhara spoke to that slayer of Daityas [Indra]: / "Having killed Bala by deceit, where will you go, lowest of the strong?
Having spoken thus to him of a hundred sacrifices [Indra], the mighty son of the ocean / covered his chariot, together with charioteer, horses, and banner, with arrows.
Wounded by arrows, Śakra fell fainted onto the chariot; / seeing that Śakra had fallen, the son of the ocean roared.
Recovering from his faint, Indra hurled his thunderbolt at Jālandhara; / then, seizing that crusher of mountains in his hand, the ocean-born one,
holding the thunderbolt under his armpit, quickly descended from his chariot; / the lord of Daityas ran forward to seize the lord of gods in battle.
Then Maghavan fled, abandoning his chariot and remembering Hari; / the arrogant son of the ocean, mounting Indra's chariot,
making Mātali his charioteer, went forward, having attained his desire. / Wherever the chariot of Indra went swiftly in the army,
mighty-armed Jālandhara himself went like a rain cloud. / Then, out of anger, Puruṣottama himself raised the sword Nandaka in battle;
urging on Garuḍa, swift as thought, he struck the Daitya army in wrath; / by force he felled chariots, horses, elephants, and hosts of foot soldiers by the thousands.

Janārdana, attended by the son of Kaśyapa [Garuḍa], performed a terrifying deed in the battle: / [he made a river] flowing with torrents of hair, bones, marrow, and blood, frequented by Piśācas, Vetālas, and birds,

filled with hands, thighs, shanks, weapons, and missiles, hard to cross, frequented by tigers and kingly elephants, / adorned with necklaces and armlets of bloody entrails, with garments of the splendor of rolling-eyed festivals.
Seeing their army slain by Viṣṇu, the foremost of the Dānavas, / by the order of Jālandhara, surrounded Hari on all sides.
Those Daityas rained streams of arrows there like rain clouds— / like bees on a lotus, like clouds upon a mountain,
like flocks of birds upon a mango tree, like a mass of smoke in the sky; / then Viṣṇu was not to be seen, nor was Tārkṣya, in the crisis of battle.
All mounted on chariots, with all manner of weapons, those great Asuras / struck the lord of Vaikuṇṭha, roaring with terrifying shouts.
Then the enemy of the Daityas [Viṣṇu], assuming a terrible form, being angered, / struck them all down in battle, as the wind fells a heap of leaves.
Then the Daitya Śailaroman ran toward Viṣṇu in anger; / even Hari's arrows were shattered upon his body.
And Śailaroman struck the body of the enemy of the Daityas with arrows; / brandishing his sword, Hari severed his head.
When the Daitya's head was cut off, the headless trunk stalked forth in battle; / and Śailaroman seized Garuḍa by both wings with his two arms.
His head flew up swiftly and fixed itself firmly back upon his shoulders; / then Hṛṣīkeśa too was astonished by his fighting there.
Seeing the head reattached, Garuḍa fell to the ground; / and leaping up again with speed, he resumed his place as head.
Then the mighty Śailaroman pulled Viṣṇu down from Garuḍa; / Hari struck him quickly with the palm of his hand, and he fell to the ground, his life departed.
Then Jālandhara spoke to his charioteer, Khaṅgaroman: / 'Drive the chariot there where Lord Janārdana is.'
At Jālandhara's command, Khaṅgaroman brought the chariot. / Seeing Viṣṇu before him, the son of the ocean spoke:
'Strike me without fear, O Viṣṇu; I will not strike you, O Mādhava.' / Hearing those words of his, with eyes reddened with rage,
Nārāyaṇa overwhelmed him with life-taking arrows; / and his limbs pierced by Viṣṇu, the ocean's valorous son
continually showered Hari with a flood of arrows; / Nārāyaṇa overwhelmed him with life-taking arrows.
Seeing Garuḍa fallen to the ground by the arrows of the ocean's son, / Janārdana called to mind his chariot situated in Vaikuṇṭha.
That chariot arrived for him, devoid of a driver, yoked with horses. / Seeing the chariot equipped with horses, the Blessed One was astonished in the battle.
Having revived Garuḍa, he appointed him to the charioteership. / Wearing a diadem on his head and the Kaustubha gem on his chest,
making the four aims of human life his horses, Hari advanced against Jālandhara, / cleaving the earth with the wheel of his chariot, along with the gods.
Swiftly he smote the army of the Dānavas with arrows. / Commanded by the king of gods, fire on the battleground
accompanied by the wind burned up the Dānava host. / Then, struck by the Blessed One along with the gods, the Daitya army
was reduced to a small remnant; seeing his own force, Jālandhara fell into contemplation. / Then the king spoke to Bhārgava: 'My army has been destroyed by the gods.
While you are present, a knower of mantras, renowned for your magical science— / what is the use of that magical science, O Brahman, or of martial power and strength,
which does not protect those afflicted with disease, or what use is strength that does not protect those who have taken refuge?' / Hearing Jālandhara's words, Bhārgava replied to him:
'Behold, O king, my power as a brāhmaṇa on the battlefield.' / Having spoken thus, touched with water and awakened by a roaring cry,
they were raised up by Kavi. Smote by clouds of life-destroying arrows, / the gods fell in the battle on all sides before the ocean's son.
Their bodies shattered by arrows, O ruler of men, they still retained their breath of life; / because of their immortality they did not die, though pierced by arrows, O best of beings.
Then Lord Nārāyaṇa spoke to Bṛhaspati: / 'Fie upon your strength, O preceptor of the gods, you who do not bring the gods back to life!'
Then Dhiṣaṇa quickly spoke to the Lord of the World: / 'Master, by means of medicinal herbs I will revive the immortals.'
Having spoken thus, Dhiṣaṇa [Bṛhaspati] also went to the Droṇa mountain, / which was situated in the Milk Ocean, and having arrived there, he took the medicinal herbs easily himself.
The preceptor revived the immortals through the application of them. / Having arisen, the gods then smote the Dānava army.
Seeing the gods risen up, the ocean-born said to Kavi: / 'Without your magical science, O Kāvya, how have these arisen?'
Hearing what was said by the demon, Śukra addressed the son of the ocean: / 'Situated in the midst of the Milk Ocean is a great mountain named Droṇa.'
Medicinal herbs abide there which bring the dead back to life. / Going there and taking a store of medicinal herbs, the preceptor of the gods
raises up with mantras the gods slain in battle.' / Hearing what Bhārgava said, the mighty one, placing the burden of the army
upon Śumbha, Jālandhara quickly went to the ocean. / Then he entered the Ocean of Milk, [to] a divine palace of great radiance.
Entering there, he beheld the pleasure-place of the Ocean of Milk, / where neither hot nor cold wind is felt, nor darkness seen,
where excellent women sing, dance, and play— / rich with the weight of plump breasts, slender-waisted, with beautiful teeth,
with coquettish dartings of eyes, with swayings of hips, / with lovely bewitching limbs, with movements of vine-like arms,
with the jingling of their footsteps, with sweet words of praise, / with fragrances and pleasing garments, with humming bee-like glances,
with the play of waving fly-whisks, with garlands, with smiling gazes— / the sportive maidens attended upon the ocean's son when he had gone there.

Eager for battle, beholding the Milk Ocean sporting there, / he bowed low and said to the Ocean of Milk: 'Father, you are destroying me! / Submerge under pretext with your waters the medicinal herbs of Mount Droṇa of your own accord.'
The Ocean of Milk said: / 'How can I submerge with my waves one who has come for refuge, my son? / The foremost sages do not praise one who abandons someone who has sought refuge.'
Hearing his uncle's words, in raging fury the Daitya king / struck the mountain continuously with a blow of his palm.
Then Mount Droṇa, O king, exceedingly terrified of Jālandhara, / assumed a form and spoke to Jālandhara:
'I have become your servant; protect me who have taken refuge. / At your command, O mighty-armed one, I will go down to the netherworld.
As long as you rule the kingdom, so long will I remain there, O lord.' / Amid the clamour of the medicinal herbs and the weeping of the Siddhas,
the mountain went down to the netherworld under the gaze of the ocean's son. / Then the hero Jālandhara returned to the great battle.
Mounting his previously prepared [chariot], he advanced toward Keśava standing in his chariot. / Seeing Mādhava standing in his chariot, the son of the river-ocean laughed aloud:
'Stay in your cart as long as I strike down these foes!' / Having spoken thus, he swiftly struck that army of the gods with arrows.
Torn apart by the arrows, the gods cried out to Bṛhaspati, 'Save us!' / Then Bṛhaspati went quickly to the Ocean of Milk.
Not seeing that Droṇa there, he became filled with anxiety, O king. / Then, returning swiftly to the battle, the lord of speech said to the immortals:
'Flee, all you gods! Mount Droṇa has perished.' / As the preceptor spoke thus, the son of the ocean cut off
his sacred thread and hair with sharp arrows, laughing at the gods. / Then the preceptor ran away at full speed, tormented by the fear of his life.
Abandoning the battle, all the gods took to flight, O king. / Having thus routed the gods, he rushed at Janārdana.
Hṛṣīkeśa too, eager for battle, rushed upon the lord of the Daityas. / Then a dreadful combat took place between Viṣṇu and Jālandhara.
The unassailable one flooded Keśava with networks of arrows. / Cleaving those arrows into pieces, and showering him with arrows, the great
Vāsudeva afflicted the asura Jālandhara with arrows. / Abandoning his chariot, his body tormented by arrows,
Jālandhara swiftly ran to conquer Viṣṇu standing in the combat. / Seeing him approaching in the battle, Hari pierced him with arrows.
Enduring the arrows of Viṣṇu in his body, he reached the vicinity of the chariot; / with one hand he [seized] Garuḍa, and with the second Hari's chariot.
Whirling [the chariot] continuously in the sky, he hurled it down onto Śvetadvīpa. / Thrown by Jālandhara's hand, Garuḍa too fell down.
On Krauñcadvīpa he took rest there for a long time. / Acyuta, fallen from that whirling circle of the chariot,
came back to the battle and said to the lord of daityas, "Stand, stand!" / Seeing Keśava, who delights in battle, come again,
the son of the ocean roared, filling the earth with arrows.

Hari swiftly pierced the daitya with a dart that flashed in his heart; then he fell. / The charioteer carried him away from the battle to his abode; [Jālandhara] said to him: "By whom have I been made shameless?"

A great battle then took place between the enemy of the daityas and Jālandhara as they stood upon the earth's surface. / Out of love for Śrī, Hari did not strike that dānava dead; he himself fell by his arrows.
Then, seeing Govinda fallen upon the earth's surface, / the daitya born of the ocean seized him and mounted his own chariot. / Then Indirā, Viṣṇu's beloved, arrived there weeping.
Kamalā stood there beside her lotus-eyed husband. / Seeing her husband fallen, Lakṣmī said to the ocean's son:
"Listen to my words, brother: Viṣṇu has been conquered and captured by you. / It is not fitting, O mighty one, to inflict widowhood upon your sister."
Hearing her words, the mighty-armed Jālandhara / released the Lord of the universe and bowed to his sister with devotion.
Out of love for his sister, he quickly bowed to Viṣṇu's feet. / Viṣṇu said to Jālandhara: "I am pleased with your deed. / Choose a boon, O lord of daityas! What boon shall I grant you?"
Jālandhara said: / "If you are pleased with me, Keśava, on account of this valor, / you must dwell in my father's abode together with Kamalā."
Saying "So be it," the bearer of the earth remembered Garuḍa, / and mounting [him], the Lord of the universe went with his beloved to the Milk Ocean.
From that time forward, Kṛṣṇa's dwelling has been in his father-in-law's home; / the Lord of gods resides in the ocean, wishing to please Lakṣmī.

6.8.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / "Having distressed the gods in battle and established Viṣṇu in his own home, / tell me, Nārada, what was done by Jālandhara, the ocean's son?"
Nārada said: / "Having bestowed gifts born of his favor upon heroes such as Śumbha, / Jālandhara then went to heaven, and upon arriving, beheld it,
where people are adorned day after day by a rain of gold, / and trees perpetually bear fruit, the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Elephants, garments, gold, milk-cows, maidens, and sesame seeds; / flowers, camphor, betel, musk, and saffron—
those great-souled ones who give these behold Amarāvatī. / By the gift of a house during the rains, by the bestowal of fire in the cold season,
by those who play all musical instruments in Śiva's temple, / and who set up a water booth in Caitra stocked with curds and boiled rice;
where they themselves swing the swinging couch, / and mynas, parrots, swans, hovering bees, and cuckoos
act as messengers and bring about reunion with the beloved; / where Rambhā is in the city, and the lovely Menakā and Tilottamā;
where are Suṣamā, Sundarī, Ghṛtācī, Puñjikasthalī, / Sukeśī, the fair-faced beautiful woman, Mañjughoṣā, and Mālinī;
and Mṛgodbhavā, Sukhadā, Dhanadaṃṣṭrā, Tilaprabhā; / those who receive the fruit of a horse sacrifice, and those who bear the fruit of a royal consecration—
where sinless apsarases by the millions disport, O king. / In this heaven of abundant happiness, the ocean-born [king] installed
Śumbha, a daitya dear as his own life, and Niśumbha as crown prince; / and coming himself from heaven to his throne, Jālandhara, the ocean-king, / ruled for two arbuda years by his own might.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / "He fought in the battle with the asuras, undefeated by the gods.
What did the glorious king, the ocean's son, do after that? / Relate that to me at length, divine sage, for I wish to hear."
Nārada said: / "Hear, O king, what was truly done by the ocean's son: / having conquered the gods in battle, he ruled his kingdom without a thorn.
Gandharvas such as Citrasena and others served the lord of asuras; / and he, the lord of asuras, enjoyed the sacrificial portions of all [the gods].
Whatever jewels and other treasures had been seized from the Milk Ocean by the gods, / the mighty one conquered them and seized all of that as well as other [riches].
While the ocean's son ruled the earth's realm, O king, / no mortal died, nor did anyone go to hell.
There was no dissension born of discord, nor any other decay from indulgence; / no woman was barren, unfortunate, or devoid of ornaments.
No woman was seen to be deformed, miserable, wicked, or infamous; / there was no widow there, nor any destitute person.
Donors were everywhere, and nowhere were there recipients [in need]; / virtuous people gave their own wealth to twice-born men.
In every house were women possessing beauty and youth; / where cow's milk, curd, and clarified butter abounded, the people were free from old age.
Auspiciousness was there for everyone, nowhere was there slaughter or bondage; / there was no injury by arrows, nor was anyone oppressed by anyone.
Debt was not seen, O king; wealthy men were on all sides; / the subjects were contented and rich in all crops everywhere, O ruler of the earth.

From the sportively planted sugarcane came sweet milk-juice, exceedingly delicious, in men's houses; / only beneficial speech of men and women was heard, and there was never a robber on the road for travelers.
Unbroken streams of clarified butter mixed with carambola fruit, / poured out and blended with sugar, fell into men's mouths from the sky on all sides simply upon remembering the ocean's son.

6.9.m: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / "What was done then, O best of the twice-born, by the gods led by Indra, / who were conquered by Jālandhara when the heavenly realm was seized?"
Nārada said: / "Then, having abandoned heaven, the gods endured misfortune for a long time; / without nectar, without sacrifices, they went to the abode of the Self-born.
In the realm of Brahmā, they saw Brahmā, the supreme lord, / harnessing his mind to the supreme self through breath-control.
All those gods, showing reverence, praised him with truthful words. / Then the blessed one was pleased and said: 'What can I do for you?'
Then the wise gods again reported to Brahmā / all about Jālandhara, as well as their own defeat.
Meditating for a moment, Brahmā went with the thirty [gods] to Kailāsa. / On the side of that mountain, filled with wonder, / the gods stood, led by Brahmā and Śakra, and praised [him]:
"Homage to Bhava, to Śarva, homage to the blue-necked one! / Homage to the gross, to the subtle, homage to the multiform one!"
Thus turning his face in all directions upon hearing the voice, Śaṅkara / said to Nandin: 'Quickly, bring the gods here.'
Hearing Śambhu's word, the gods were quickly summoned by Nandin. / Entering the inner apartment, the gods beheld [him] with wonder-struck eyes:
Śaṅkara seated there on a throne, the causer of prosperity to the world, / attended indeed by thousands of crores of devoted Gaṇas,
naked, deformed, crooked, matted-haired, and dusky with dust. / Bowing down before him together with the gods, the Grandfather spoke:
"Just as Śakra had an illness of pleasure, so has he now come in vain. / Show mercy, O Mahādeva, affectionate to those who seek refuge!"
Then, hearing the loud laughter of the all-pervading wielder of Pināka, Brahmā / said to the lord of the gods of gods, "Behold the condition of the celestials!"
Then the lord of all, Parameśvara, knowing the heart's desire of Brahmā / and the crushing of Śakra's pride for the sake of the gods,
requested lovingly by Bhavānī, O king, Hara spoke this word: / "That enemy who was not slain by Viṣṇu, how can he be slain by me?
The previously created weapons such as the thunderbolt and others, O Grandfather— / by those weapons that powerful asura Jālandhara cannot at all be killed.
He cannot be slain by weapons previously fashioned, even by me. / Let the gods make a firm weapon capable of enduring my life-force."
Hearing this reply of Śambhu, Brahmā then said to Śaṅkara: / "Make the great weapon yourself; you know your own strength."
Hearing his speech, Maheśvara replied: / 'O Brahmā, release your fiery energy filled with wrath along with the gods.'
Then Brahmā, indicating the Brahmāstra, released his fiery energy; / Rudra then himself released the fiery energy born of his third eye.
And all the gods angrily discharged their mass of fiery energy. / In the meantime, remembered by Hara, Madhusūdana arrived.
Addressed by him, "What shall I do?", Śiva said to Janārdana: / "O Viṣṇu, why was Jālandhara not slain by you in battle?
Why, abandoning the gods, did you go to sleep on the ocean of milk?"
The glorious Viṣṇu said: "If I slay him, O lord of gods, how could Śrī remain my beloved? / Therefore, O beloved of Pārvatī, slay Jālandhara in battle!"

"Release the fiery energy born of wrath," Keśava was thus addressed by Śarva. / He released the Vaiṣṇava fiery energy, and all of it increased together. / Seeing that vast, all-pervading fiery energy, he said to Keśava:
Śaṅkara said: "With this fiery energy you ought swiftly to make a weapon for me." / Hearing that speech of Śaṅkara, Viśvakarman and the others,
looked at one another, apprehensive, wondering, "What shall we do?" / Seeing them standing silent and knowing what was in their minds,
Lord Brahmā then said: "It is unendurable even to deities; / they are unable to bear that fiery energy, and by whom can it be held?"
Then the Lord, laughing and leaping up over the fiery energy, / Śambhu danced a series of pirouettes on the heel of his left foot.
Then the gods, Mahendra and the others, seeing Śaṅkara dancing / above the fiery energy at that time, joyfully played musical instruments.
From that time forward, a series of pirouettes is whirled in dances. / Then a discus was produced from the trampling and dancing of Śambhu,
provided with three hundred thousand spokes and crowded with a crore of points. / From the rubbing of Śarva's foot, sparks issued from that fiery energy,
and with it Viśvakarman fashioned weapons and aerial chariots. / Then those celestials, out of fear upon seeing the Sudarśana discus,
said to the lord of gods, "Save us! Save us!", O king. / Taking the hardness of the earth and also the brilliance of iron,
the sheath which was made by Viśvakarman was burned to ashes; / by that discus which was created, Kāla, being burned, fell to the ground.
Then Dhūrjaṭi placed that discus in the hand of Brahmā. / Seeing his beard singed by the masses of rays from the discus, the lord of Umā,
laughing, took the discus swiftly from the hand of Brahmā; / Śiva placed the discus in his armpit, like a poor man hiding a treasure.
Then the discus, resting in Śiva's armpit, was no longer seen, / like the fruit of a gift given to a great fool.

6.10.m: Nārada said: / Following this, having gone to the son of the Ocean, it was told by me: / "A vow has been made by Śambhu to slay you, O lord of all heroes." / Having heard this word of mine, O king, the asura then asked:
Jālandhara said: "What collection of gems is there in the house of the trident-wielder, O great sage? / Tell all of that to me; there is no fight without a prize."
Nārada said: "Ashes upon his body, an old bull, snakes on his limbs, poison in his throat, / an alms-bowl in his hand, two sons—Gajānana and the six-faced one;
Such is his grandeur; listen to what else there is from me: / the daughter of the king of mountains, wide-eyed and high-breasted—
by whose beauty even the Lord, though he had burned the god of love, was enchanted; / for whose diversion Maheśa constantly performs amusing plays.
Dancing and singing to them, Śambhu himself becomes a jester. / She is famous as Pārvatī, the goddess who is the very boundary of beauty.
Vṛndā, the excellent woman, O king, and these auspicious apsarases— / they do not equal even a sixteenth fraction of Pārvatī."
Having spoken thus, O ruler of the earth, to the intolerant Jālandhara, / I vanished in an instant before the eyes of all the demons.
Then that son of the Ocean sent the son of Siṃhikā as an envoy. / Reaching Kailāsa in an instant, he saw the dwelling of the gods.
Meanwhile, Hari, taking leave of the terrible Hara, / went swiftly and unseen to the milk ocean out of fear of a schism.
Rāhu beheld the intensely radiant mansion of Śaṅkara. / Looking at himself with his own eyes, greatly amazed, he wondered, "What is this?"
Wishing to enter, he was blocked at the door by the powerful doorkeepers. / Though forbidden, he still made an attempt; then they raised their weapons.

Restraining those Gaṇas, Nandī addressed the afflicter of the moon: / "Who are you? Why have you come here? What is your business, O barbarian? / State your business before the terrifying Gaṇas slay you!"
Rāhu said: "I am the messenger of Jālandhara; take me to Śarva. / The business of the great king must not be spoken to a doorkeeper in between."
Nandī, hearing what the messenger said, went to Nīlalohita; / bowing like a rod before him and standing, he said to Śaṅkara:
"The son of Siṃhikā, O great king, stands at the door on business. / May he enter, or let him depart; you ought to command."
Then, hearing what was spoken by Nandin, Maheśvara, as if in haste, / having sent the sleeping goddess away from the inner apartment, surrounded by her female companions,
then said to the doorkeeper: "Nandin, bring in the messenger." / Then the mighty Nandin, taking that messenger by the hand,
brought him into the midst of the gods and showed him Śambhu. / Rāhu then beheld him in his mind as matted-haired, dark-blue,
five-faced, ten-armed, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, / bereft of the goddess, adorned on his head with the crescent moon,
attended by multitudes of serpents issuing forth with each out-breath, / surrounded by all the hosts of gods, and attended by crores of Gaṇas.
Then, knowing the messenger had arrived, Śambhu looked directly before him / and said, 'Speak!' Then Rāhu began to speak.
Rāhu said: 'O god, I have been sent into your presence by Jālandhara. / Hearing his auspicious words through my mouth, act quickly!
O Giriśa, you are intent on austerities, without qualities, devoid of dharma. / You have no father, no mother, and are devoid of wealth, lineage, and the like.
The mighty-armed Jālandhara enjoys the three worlds. / You too are under his command; therefore, do as he has said!
How can you, an ancient man, be lustful and ride a bull?' / While he was speaking thus, the two sons, Skanda and Vināyaka, arrived.
At that time, the god of gods, having restrained his speech, rubbed his body / with dispersed movements of his hands, and Vāsuki fell to the ground.
Then the tail of the mouse, the mount of Heramba, was seized by the serpent. / Seeing his own vehicle seized, [Heramba] said, 'Let go, let go!'
Meanwhile, seeing Skanda's mount agitated and screeching loudly, / Vāsuki, out of fear of it, vomited up the seized tail of the mouse.
Then, climbing Hara's body, he remained coiled around his neck. / Then, from the winds of his breath, a fire was born.
By its heat, the crescent moon situated in the forest of matted locks / attained moistness, so that his body was flooded, as it were.
Indeed, by its streams of nectar, the garland of heads of Brahmā— / the skulls upon Hara's head—was then brought back to life.
It recited the entire order of yoga and the Vedas previously studied. / Hearing each other's recitations, the heads then began to argue:
'I am the beginning! I am the first! I alone am higher than the highest! / I am the creator! I am the protector!'—thus eager with one another.
[Other heads] grieve: 'Nothing was given by me, nothing was enjoyed, nothing was offered into the fire! / With a mind seized by greed, no wealth was offered to the brāhmaṇa!'
Then, from the matted locks of the Lord, a great gaṇa manifested: / three-faced, three-footed, three-tailed, and having seven arms.
He was named Kīrtimukha, tawny, having matted hair, and huge. / Seeing him, that row of skulls stood as if dead with fear.
Then that gaṇa, Kīrtimukha, bowing down before the Lord, the auspicious god, / said in front [of him]: 'O Lord, I am exceedingly hungry!'
Then Śaṅkara said: 'O, eat those who are slain in battle!' / Reflecting for a moment, and seeing no battle anywhere at that time,
the gaṇa approached to eat Brahmā, but was restrained by Śaṅkara. / Then, all his own limbs were eaten by Kīrtimukha,
who was intensely starving and forbidden on every side. / Seeing then that boldness and the devotion of Kīrtimukha,
the Lord, pleased, said to him: 'Always remain in my temple! / Whoever comes into my abode lacking devotion to you
shall fall quickly.' Having been addressed thus, he vanished. / Then the gods showered showers of flowers upon Śambhu's head.
Having witnessed such an immense wonder in the assembly of the bearer of the trident, / Svarbhānu, amazed, spoke once more to the lord of gods:
'How do passions forcibly touch you, a self-controlled yogin? / You are indeed worshipped by the sense-organs; how can you be attained by sense-objects?
You accept worship on all sides from the world-protectors, Brahmā and the rest. / You do not look upon any god, nor do you worship anyone.
How are you established in the world as the Lord, while eating alms? / O king of yogins, you hide Gaurī; give the lovely one to me!
Together with your two sons, Skanda and the pot-bellied [Gaṇeśa], / take your begging bowl now and wander constantly from house to house!'
In this manner, Rāhu said many things to the Lord. / The Blessed One, having heard it, spoke no answer at all.
Then, turning away from the silent Lord, Rāhu said to Nandin: / 'You are his minister, his general, bearing the reflection of his fierce face.
You ought to instruct him who has fallen from proper conduct in this way; / otherwise, out of fury, he will fall slain in battle like Indra.'
Hearing his words, Nandin informed the lord; / and knowing the will of the Trident-bearer [Śiva] by a mere knit of his brow,

Nandin, the leader of the gaṇas, honoured Rāhu and sent him off. / Then, going to Jālandhara, / Svarbhānu related to him in detail that account and the captivating beauty of Gaurī.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, named 'The Return of Rāhu from Kailāsa', in the narrative of Jālandhara in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses].
