मेरोर्मंदरकंदरेप्रतिरवानुत्थापयन्वारणान्
6.11.m:
Nārada said: / Then, having heard the words of the messenger, the glorious Jālandhara / summoned his entire army and set out on his march. / Then the sound of the armies gathered from here and there was heard,

waking the Kinnaras sleeping with their women in the caves of Mandara, / causing the elephants in the caves of Meru and Mandara to awaken with echoes;
Crowds of lions abandoned their path before [it]—such a clamour of the mighty army deafened the three worlds.
Then arose the sound of drums at the seat, O King, of Jālandhara, / with that great sound dear to warriors.
Towering mountains trembled, and palaces shook. / From the bellies of the seven oceans, the Daityas and Dānavas emerged,
armoured and roaring loudly, equipped with various vehicles. / A great roar went forth as the neighing of horses sounded outside and in front.
The earth was shaken by the wheels of chariots, and / the earth, together with its forests, was covered by the marching herds of elephants.
Driven by Jālandhara, terrible warriors stood upon ten thousand chariots; / there were two thousand hundred-millions of horses, and a hundred million elephants.

An army of one hundred thousand charioteers with banners shone; / nine hundred and fifty million principal leaders were seen. / The mighty army set forth, shrouding the sun with its parasols.

In some places it was like a forest of pale, yellowish lotuses because of the white parasols; / in other places it became like blooming blue water-lilies because of the parasols of peacock feathers.
In his march, the sky was clouded in some places with rising clouds of dust, / and in others, it was like a lake with waves through the surging banners of cloth.
The earth was made of elephants and horses, the sky of banners and parasols, / and the circle of directions of chowries, as the Daitya army marched forward.
Then the Daitya Jālandhara, eager to set out, / placed upon his shoulder his spear adorned with various jewels,
and came to ask leave of the great Viṣṇu, who dwells in the ocean. / Bowing, Jālandhara then spoke this to Hari:
'What shall I provide for your enjoyment? Tell me, O gracious one!' / Hearing the words of the ocean-born one, Nārāyaṇa, filled with joy,
said: 'What pleasing thing, desired by the son of the ocean, can I do?' / Thus addressed, highly delighted, he quickly spoke to Hari:
'I am going to fight in battle; stay happily here in the ocean.' / Bestowed with unbroken grains of rice by Lakṣmī and honoured by Keśava,
he departed from the abode of Hari and came to take leave of the Ocean. / Bowing to the Ocean, he said: 'Father, I am going far away.'

"You ought to grant me permission to conquer the blue-throated [Śiva] in battle."
Having heard the words of his son who was eager to march against Śaṅkara,

he was addressed by the king of the ocean: "Son, leave that ascetic alone!
Enjoy the kingdom given by me; leave that ascetic far away!

Your prowess is very wondrous; there is no king equal to you.
By you, dear child, the earth has been raised higher than heaven.

In your kingdom, the earth shines like Vaikuṇṭha itself;
the god who was unconquerable by the Daityas has been brought [here] at once along with Śrī.

Live near me, child; leave the beggar Śaṅkara alone."
Though spoken to thus by the ocean, [Jālandhara], full of passion for Girijā,

disregarded his father’s words. Having gone to his own warriors,
and made ready for battle, Vṛndā sang [these words] to Jālandhara:

Vṛndā said:
"O lord, supreme king, no battle should be fought with a base ascetic!
Let your mind be turned back; see how it is drawn toward Pārvatī!

Why do you desire Gaurī? Is Pārvatī superior to me?
She is an ascetic woman, without support, ever attached to a post [or Śiva].

Affectionate toward children, [yet] barren, she thus has a mock-child;
she was praised in vain by Nārada. Abandon her and love me!"
Hearing Vṛndā's words, the son of the ocean replied: / 'Without having seen the beauty of Pārvatī, my mind does not turn back.'

O Vṛndā, you must protect the realm and the capital!
I should be constantly remembered, O fierce woman, if Śaṅkara should slay me."
Hearing the words of her husband, Vṛndā, accompanied by a smile, / then mounted a palanquin and went to the sacred seat of Jālandhara.

Nārada said:
Then the son of the ocean, endowed with great might, set out for Kailāsa,
surrounded by an army of sixty thousand mahāpadmas.

Meanwhile, having abandoned Kailāsa, Śaṅkara went away,
accompanied by his troops, sons, and beloved, to Kailāsa upon Mānasottara.

Then Jālandhara reached Kailāsa on the first day;
having stationed his armies, he was eager to behold Kailāsa.

The winds blew, wrapped in heaps of celestial pollen of Mandāra flowers,
curved by showers of cool water-spray,

where handsome winds blew, rippling with the high, swelling breasts of Siddha women,
rich with the nectar of Mandāra blossoms,

and where, beholding the array of women's footsteps glossy with the luster of Aśoka blooms,
the lord of the Dānavas was overwhelmed with desire.

There the gods obtain delight, gladdened by seeing their own reflections,
where the lusters of the beloved women of the Kinnaras are displayed in lovemaking,

where Mandāra trees shine everywhere with shed sprouts,
where trees crowded with various creepers are overrun by Śambhu's attendants,

where, seeing all the fragrance of the women, a friend to their consummate radiance,
I think musk, as if having embraced them for the amusement of the mind, plunges into blackness.

In some places [adorned with] a lotus shining like the best red chalk, / in other places moving cakora birds perched on clove leaves.
in another place was an earring gleaming like the sun on the bank of a mountain stream, and in another place were bees bowed with humility before a swaying Nicula blossom-cluster;

in one place fresh mango sprouts were agitated by cooing cuckoos; in another place the roots of sturdy rice plants were frequented by herds of deer;
in another place the forest, sanctified by the footsteps of the finest beautiful celestial wives, brings agitation to the minds of even sages here.

Having thus beheld the abode of Hara endowed with these qualities,
and the wondrous Kailāsa, a receptacle of all gems,

the exceedingly astonished Daitya spoke to the son of Bhṛgu:
"Father, why do people like you speak of him as an ascetic,

he whose wife is of such a kind and whose home is so captivating?
Not seeing Śambhu there, tell me, O poet, where has Hara gone?

How is it so, if out of fear of me?" Thus asked, the descendant of Bhṛgu replied:
"O king, Śambhu has gone to the great, inaccessible mountain Mānasottara;

Mahādeva has gone there, and it is impossible for others to go [there]."
Having heard the words of Kāvya [Śukra], the mighty Daitya said:

Jālandhara said:
"I will go to the lord of the gods; go before me, descendant of Bhṛgu!"
Having said this, he set out to the place where Śaṅkara himself was.

The son of the ocean saw that best of mountains, Mānasottara;
its height was sixty thousand yojanas.

That mountain Mānasottara, O king, was surrounded by the Daitya armies;
many Daitya kings quickly climbed the mountain.

Darkness was spread by parasols, and trembling arose from the sound of musical instruments;
the clamor of their armies filled heaven and earth.

Nārada said:
Then, seeing that great army of Daityas arrived thus,
having placed Gaurī, surrounded by her female companions, on a very high peak of the mountain,

the blessed Śiva, surrounded by all his attendants equipped for battle, wild with fight,
thirty thousand mahāpadmas of Pramathas,

Śambhu said to Nandin, the chief of his gaṇas: "By you
the mighty Daitya, the hero Jālandhara, must be struck down in battle.

Go, surrounded by heroes such as Mahākāla and the others;
therefore, you must fight in battle with great valor,

until through battle the victory over the enemy shall be mine, O hero!"
Having heard these words of Śambhu, he spoke to his charioteer:

"O wise one, bring my chariot today, [you] Crow-faced one!"
Having heard Nandin’s words, he brought the chariot,

fitted with thirty-two horses, equipped with sixteen wheels,
provided with sixty banners, measuring thirty-two yojanas,

filled with all weapons, a battle chariot ready.
To protect Nandin's wheels, Śaṅkara commanded his two sons,

Skanda and Vināyaka; both equipped and mounted on their own vehicles.
Nandin, surrounded by the gaṇas, having honored the Lord with praises,

mounted his chariot and went forth against the Dānavas.
Over his head shone a parasol measuring twelve yojanas.

As soon as Nandin went out, those Dānavas were already before [him];
the Dānavas of terrible appearance had climbed up onto the mountain.

Struck by the sharp weapons of the gaṇas, they fell to the ground;
being slain by the gaṇas, the Daityas abandoned the mountain from afar.

Then, having descended from that mountain together like smoke,
the gaṇas, O king, smote the mighty Daityas with sharp weapons.

Seeing [the mountain] covered with immortals, the Daitya soldiers held their ground;
then a battle took place between the gaṇas and the Dānavas.

Then there was a very fierce shower of arrows of the Dānavas and the gods;
then the crow-faced ones smote all the elephants in battle,

the mighty ones [destroyed] chariots, horses, and foot-soldiers;
of the multitudes of Daityas possessing great sorcery slain in combat,

the sky was filled with their fearsome, laughing heads,
with disheveled hair, red faces, and terrible fangs and eyes.

The earth was strewn everywhere with headless trunks red with blood,
severed at the shanks, thighs, waists, and backs by lions.

Then a very great clamor arose in the armies of the demon lords as they fled, / whose soldiers were struck down by Śambhu's attendants, like oceans roaring at the end of a cosmic age.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled “Defeat of the Demon Army,” in the Jālandhara story in the dialogue between Nārada and Yudhiṣṭhira, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the collection of fifty thousand verses.

6.12.m: Nārada said: / Seeing the demon army slain by the attendants led by Nandin, / the demons, Śumbha and the others, became enraged and marched against the attendants.
Then Śumbha, the great demon, fought against Nandin, / and Niśumbha fought against Mahākāla, and Kāla against Lokeśvara in the battle.
Śailaroman fought Puṣpadanta, the mighty Kolāhala fought Mālyavant, / having arrived in the battle by the power of illusion, O king.
Bhayānaka ran against Caṇḍa, and Rāhu against Skanda; / Sarparoman went against Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Ghardhara against Madana.
Ketumukha went to kill Śubha, and Jambha went against Vināyaka; / Pātālaketu went against Hāsa, and Romakaṇṭaka against Bhṛṅgīśa.
In their millions, Rudra's attendants and the demons fought with one another / while their two masters watched on in that battle.
Striking with firm blows, the demon hosts then attacked with arrows. / Nandin released those arrows like a heavy downpour on a mountain.
Then he filled Śumbha's mouth with arrows, / just as the wind fills a cave of Mount Mandara with heaps of leaves.
Śumbha then abandoned his bow, rushed at him from his chariot, / and uprooting a mountain, struck Nandin in the chest with it.
Having pierced Nandin's chest and pulverized the chariot in battle, / that mountain fell to the ground like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Falling into a swoon, he regained consciousness in a moment and fled swiftly. / Mahākāla was struck in the chest with a club by Niśumbha.
Approaching, he struck the demon on top of his crown with a mace. / Disregarding that blow, the very powerful Niśumbha,
that mighty one seized Mahākāla by the feet, / whirled him around from the palm of his hand, threw him down, and roared.
He, having swallowed the wind of his mouth, roared, red with blood. / And Puṣpadanta was struck in the face with a fist by Śailaroman;
having struck Śailaroman with a mace, he knocked him down to the ground. / Seeing him fallen to the ground, the very powerful Giriketu
pounded the formidable Puṣpadanta with a club. / Then Puṣpadanta cut off Giriketu's head with a sword.
Taking up shield and sword, he ran toward Giriketu. / The head said to him: “Why do you leave me, who desire battle, and go away?
Are you not ashamed to run when this body is headless?” / When that was said by the head, Puṣpadanta was seized by the feet
by that headless trunk, and he slashed its belly with a sharp sword. / Out of the belly came forth a mighty demon with a hundred heads,
endowed with two hundred eyes, teeming with two hundred arms. / O king, rolling along, his head came near to the headless trunk.
Seeing that head arrive, Puṣpadanta cut it with his sword. / Then a terrible demon of fever, named Bhūkampana [arose].
Then Puṣpadanta was crushed there by the two of them, O king; / and tormented by that unbearable, swift-moving fever,
Śiva's attendant abandoned the fight and fled trembling to the mountain. / The great archer Kolāhala with three arrows
pierced Mālyavant in both shoulders and on the forehead, and then the demon / was struck by arrows from Mālyavant with various kinds of sharp weapons.
Kolāhala struck back, displaying his own agility. / He too, casting off the pain of the weapons, that Mālyavant, leader of the attendants,
took up a mountain and with it struck Kolāhala in battle. / From him came forth a frightful fever named Jvalana,
having three heads, nine arms, and nine feet, exceedingly tawny. / That fever bewildered Mālyavant with its splendor.
Overcome, Mālyavant abandoned the battle and went to the mountain. / In the battle Caṇḍi was struck in the heart with a noose by Bhayānaka;
a horse came forth from it, and he too was thrown into the ocean. / In the battle Kārttikeya struck Rāhu with sharp arrows;
and having covered him with a mass of arrows, he quickly hurled a spear. / Seeing that great spear flying, blazing as if with brilliance,
Rāhu leaped into the sky and swiftly caught it with both hands. / Having caught that spear, roaring loudly again and again,
Svarbhānu struck him on the head with his own spear. / When his chest was struck with the spear, a river issued from his body;
in the battle, Mahādeva's son was flooded by it. / Somehow that river was checked, and, with his army broken, he went to the mountain.
Hearing the harsh cry of the swarm of troops out of distress, the ocean-born [Jālandhara] / did not even remember that master of cuckoos, skilled in words of sweet voice.
Barbara slew with a sword Dahana, who was scattering arrows. / Kūṣmāṇḍa was then struck on the head with a fist by Sarparoman.
Hāsa was struck with a club by Pātālaketu. / Emerging from his body, an elephant shattered the club.
It was struck on the trunk with a blow of the fist by Pātālaketu. / Romakaṇṭaka battered Bhṛṅgīśa with weapons.
Bhṛṅgīśa too, terrified of the battle, went in haste straight to the mountain. / Suddenly the smoke-colored and white [one] fell into Ketumukha's mouth;
the huge-bodied, large-mouthed demon swallowed the attendant. / There was a great cry of woe when he was swallowed by Ketu in the battle.
Then Vināyaka, his body pierced by the sharp arrows of Jṛmbha, / cut off the trunk of that elephant[-demon] with an axe.
Then the demon Jṛmbha struck the belly of the pot-bellied god with a spear. / The mouse also, pierced by arrows, entered the mouth of a cave.
Vināyaka, afflicted by blows, lamented frantically in the battle: / “Alas, Mother! Alas, Father! Alas, Brother! Alas, my dear mouse!”
Hearing the cry of Gaṇeśa, the goddess, / coming from another peak, Pārvatī then said to Śiva:
“Heramba is being killed by the demons, and Skanda too has been struck down! / Śiva, why do you sport on the mountain? Protect your two sons and the attendants as well!
Today is the very moment for the weapons, the trident and others, that you constantly hold!” / Then, having heard Gaurī's words, Śiva said to Vīrabhadra:
“Let the bull be readied quickly!” When this was said, he prepared it then: / he bound a crown radiant as the sun upon its two horns;
tying a hundred bells around its neck, two mirrors were placed upon its ears, / a network of small bells on its shoulder, and a large anklet on its foot,
a thousand chowries on its tail, and eight nooses on its mouth. / And then the auspicious Goddess stood at Śarva's side,
endowed with eight nooses, and bearing a sword there, Ambikā. / All weapons were placed [upon it], and that bull shone forth, all readied.
Then he was adorned by Pārvatī with her own garland of bells; / and an auspicious mark was made by the goddess, and it was addressed with honor:
“O lord of bulls, Hara must not be abandoned by you in the crisis of battle; / having conquered the enemies in combat, you must return along with Śambhu.”
Hearing the words of the goddess, Hara then mounted his bull; / having taken a thousand weapons and adorned with his own ornaments, / he said respectfully to Pārvatī: 'I am going to battle.'

The Lord said:
"You remain here, alone in your true form, though full of longing, O passionate lady; / for the Dānavas have assembled with evil designs.

Therefore you must protect yourself by yourself, O fair-faced lady."
Having said this, Rudra mounted the bull and went to the battlefield.
Surrounded by thirty thousand great lotuses of Pramathas, Śiva advanced. / Swiftly Vīrabhadra, mounted on a chariot drawn by lions, in great haste,
the hero protects the left side of Maheśa, O king. / Maṇibhadra, slayer of enemy heroes, in a chariot drawn by horses,
bearing a bow, protects the right side of Dhūrjaṭi. / Having descended from the lofty lord of mountains, he reached the battle together with the Gaṇas.
Seeing Maheśāna mounted upon the bull, the Daityas roared. / Then arose a mighty clamour between the armies of the Daityas and the Pramathas.
A terrible clash took place between the two, O king. / Then Nandī, Mahākāla, Kāla, and the mighty Skaṇda,
Mālyavān, Puṣpadanta, Vṛṣalī, Svarṇadantika, / Caṇḍīśa, Madana, Caṇḍa, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Guptalomaka,
all those who were previously routed in battle, arrived at the press of battle. / In front of Śiva those mighty Daityas fought.
A fearsome battle took place between the Gaṇas and the Dānava warriors. / Then those mighty ones, having routed the army of the Gaṇas,
surrounded Śiva on all sides in battle with floods of arrows, / with pikes, spears, maces, mallets, and iron bars,

just as the senses surround the self with the five sense objects each. / Then Śambhu struck down the Daityas in battle with exceedingly fierce arrows, / just as the month of Māgha swiftly destroys sins in a moment by a bath.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, entitled "The Coming of the Glorious Mahādeva to the Battle," in the story of Jālandhara in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand [verses], in the dialogue between Nārada and Yudhiṣṭhira.

6.13.m:
Nārada said:
Then Jālandhara, hearing the clamour of the Daityas in battle, / arrived mounted on a chariot where the god Sadāśiva was.
In anger he quickly said to his charioteer, Khaṅgaroman: / "Drive the chariot swiftly, harnessed with a thousand horses!
With valor I will kill that ascetic adorned with matted locks, ashes, and bones! / What power does that cripple, mounted on a bull, have in battle with me?"

Nārada said:
Having spoken thus and addressed Khaṅgaroman, the haughty one, / taking up his dreadful bow, rushed swiftly in his chariot.
Vīrabhadra then blocked him as he came with sharp arrows. / Though his body was made breathless and covered with arrows,
even if the retinue of the Lord of Creatures was equal to the gods, / yet can skulls ever bear comparison to the moon, the treasure of the digits?
Maṇibhadra also pierced the son of the Ocean with arrows. / But striking Maṇibhadra with a noose, he said these words to the Lord:
"Come to fight, Mahādeva, if you have practice with weapons! / You strike me, but I will not strike the bearer of matted locks first!"
As he was speaking thus out of arrogance, Vīrabhadra, full of wrath, / filled him with arrows, as the sun [fills] a lotus with its rays.
Then Maṇibhadra with his mace struck down his army, / chariot upon chariot, hero, horse upon horse;
slaying elephant upon elephant, he felled them to the earth. / In an instant the ground became impassable, red with mud of blood.
From the mountain, the leaders of the Gaṇas also slew the Dānavas in battle. / The valiant Dānavas fell to the surface of the earth, their life-breaths gone.
With headless trunks, stout arms, and severed heads, and with the backs, trunks, and thighs of elephants, / the valiant Dānavas fell, filling the earth, O king.

Nārada said:
Having seen Hara thus in battle, exceedingly difficult to conquer, / and having also observed other omens in the world—
a strange brilliance in the gods, the stars, the moon, and all things, / the sphere of the universe unfolded, a strange splendour of the sun—
broken, Jālandhara then thought again, O king: / "I have not seen that Gaurī of whom Nārada spoke to me.
How will I now see Umā stationed in her eternal abode? / Indeed, I shall go to see her first; afterwards I will fight with Śambhu."
Having reflected thus in his mind, the son of the Ocean spoke to the Daitya, / to Śumbha, a hero who conquers the fierce, equal in prowess to himself:
"Assuming a form resembling mine, you ought to fight. / This burden of battle, of the camp and of the army, is yours.
I will go to see that Gaurī who captivates my mind." / Having spoken thus, he then gave him the ornaments, taking them from his own body.
Giving him his armour, weapons, and chariot together with the charioteer, / the son of the ocean, accompanied by Durvāraṇa, left the army.
Having gone unseen from there to a secret cave, O king, / on the Mānasottara mountain, he assumed the form of Hara.
When Durvāraṇa had assumed a form resembling Nandī, / the disguised Śaṅkara and Nandī then climbed the mountain
on whose peak Gaurī was staying together with her female companions, O king. / Seeing him approaching, pierced by arrows, leaning on the shoulder of Nandī,
and seeing his garments smeared with blood, Bhavānī was astounded. / Her companions, Jayā and the rest, approached him in agitation.
Going near to Śaṅkara, they asked him, deeply sorrowful: / "What has happened to you, Lord of the Gods? By whom have you been defeated in battle?
Why do you, pierced by darts, weep like a worldly man, O Lord?" / Thus addressed, he gave them his ornaments one by one,
slowly taking them off his body, Vāsuki and the rest. / And seeing the severed heads of Gaṇeśa and Skanda at his side,
Ambikā wept: "Alas, Skanda! Alas, Gaṇeśa! Alas, Rudra!" / Then all her companions wept, wasted with grief.
Here Nandī said to Jayā: "You look after him! / Maṇibhadra, Vīrabhadra, and the mighty Puṣpadanta,
Dambhana, Dhūmatimira, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and the others were slain in battle; / Caṇḍī, Bhṛṅgī, Kirīṭin, and Mahākāla and Śṛṅkhalin,
Caṇḍīśa, Guptanetra, and Kāla and the rest were slain in battle. / As I roamed about, the two heads of Vināyaka and Skanda
were seen by me in the great battle, O goddess." Having said this, he cast them before her. / Hearing those words of Nandī, taking the two heads of her sons,
Pārvatī wailed loudly, crying out: "O son! O son! / O foe of Tāraka, how were you slain in battle by the son of the Ocean?
You indeed were consecrated by the gods as commander-in-chief after three days; / how then, O hero, was the one named Tāraka struck down by you [then]?
Were you abandoned by the Blue-Throated Lord, since you have fallen to the earth? / And the face of a daughter-in-law was not seen by me, O sons, unfortunate that I am!
The pleasures of worldly life that exist were not enjoyed by you, my child! / O father, Heramba, Lord of Obstacles, Pot-bellied, Elephant-faced!
By whom on the battlefield was my son struck down, who is worshiped by the Siddhas? / Where is that mount, the mouse, my child? By whom was it harmed?"
Wailing thus, Gaurī spoke to Śiva, who was deeply sorrowful: / "You are Rudra incarnate, Lord of the Gods, Hara! Do not fear!"
“Where has the bull gone, O Lord? Has he been slain by Jālandhara? / What can I do to please you, whose body is mangled with arrows?”
Hearing the goddess’s words, Śaṅkara sighed deeply / and said: “Our two sons have been slain; why do you grieve in vain, my beloved?

Now, O goddess, you ought to save me by the contact of your limbs.” / Hearing Śaṅkara's words, which were inappropriate to the occasion and distressed, / Ambikā replied to the god, speaking words that were not agreeable:

“In great despondency, when ruin has fallen, in fear, while absorbed in meditation, during vomiting, during severe fever, / at a śrāddha, on a journey, and in the presence of a guru or elders, the wise shun sexual pleasure, O Śaṅkara.
How can you solicit me, who am distressed with grief upon grief, afflicted with mourning for my sons, / withered, pale with tears, and distraught?”
Hearing these words of Bhavānī, the illusory Maheśvara, / seeking his own purpose, infatuated by Gaurī's beauty, said:
“If women do not grant pleasure to an afflicted man, / they will surely fall into the terrible Raurava hell; of this there is no doubt.
I am deprived of my gaṇas, deprived of my sons, deprived of my wits, O fair-faced woman! / At present I am deprived of my home; I am deprived of everything, O beautiful one!
I am stripped of a good life, and have come here to ask you; / entering my house quickly, I abandon my own nature.
Arise, Nandin, let us go together to the tīrtha; go ahead! / Go as you please, beloved; renounce your own nature!”
Hearing these words of the illusory Maheśa, Ambikā then / drew a long, heavy sigh and was numbed with grief.

In his extreme agitation, she said nothing for a moment. / She by whom the entire universe, moving and unmoving, is deluded— / she herself was deluded by him, and did not recognize her own grief.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, entitled “The Arrival of Jālandhara as the Illusory Maheśa,” in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.
